newsitem.title: UK: UK's Clarke says UK could be in first EMU wave - FT.
newsitem.headline: UK's Clarke says UK could be in first EMU wave - FT.

text.p: The UK could be in the first group of countries to join European monetary union (EMU) if the ruling Conservatives are re-elected, UK Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke told the Financial Times newspaper.
"Yes, it is possible we could join the first wave" Clarke told the FT in an interview.

Although Clarke reiterated the UK government stance that EMU is unlikley to go ahead on the scheduled January 1, 1999 start date, he said he believed EMU would start in the lifetime of the next UK parliament.
When asked if the first wave of EMU would happen in the next parliament, Clarke said, "Yes, I think the chances are that it will start in the next parliament."
Prime Minister John Major is scheduled to call a general election by May.
On the UK economy, Clarke said there was evidence the economy was strengthening but there was no sign of an 1980s-style boom.
"I think everything shows a strengthening recovery, not out of hand, not showing symptoms of a boom and not building up inflationary pressures," he said.
Clarke said he was under no pressure to raise interest rates before the election, although he did not rule one out.
The FT said the Chancellor criticised the Bank of England for paying too much attention to financial futures markets in saying interest rates would have to rise.
Clarke said it was "nonsense" to suggest the recent rise of the pound would have no impact in dampening inflation.
"It must be nonsense to assert that such a dramatic strengthening of the exchange rate has no anti-inflation affect," he said.
Sterling has risen up to 6.6 percent against a trade- weighted basket of currencies since October, gaining as much as 14.4 percent against the German mark during that period.
Clarke decided to leave interest rates unchanged at his monthly meeting with George on January 15 and said since that the strong pound was the key influence in keeping rates steady.
Last week Bank of England governor Eddie George called for a "modest pre-emptive" rate rise.
UK base lending rates are currently 6.0 percent and were last raised by a quarter of a percentrage point on October 30.
